Operation Christmas Child is a Samaritan’s Purse project that works with local churches and ministries overseas to distribute gift-filled shoeboxes to children at Christian outreach events. Shetler suggested packing school supplies, hygiene items, a toy or craft kit and something to wear, such as a hat or gloves. Donors can choose to pack for a child ages two to four, five to nine or 10 to 14. Shetler asked donors to leave out candy, liquids, toothpaste, soap, glass items and war-themed toys. Shetler thanked Williams Lake residents for their generosity over the years. “It’s such an expression of love and compassion to children around the world that do not have much,” she said. Empty shoeboxes and brochures are available at the Evangelical Free Church, 1100 North 11th Ave., and at Kit and Kaboodle, 83A Second Ave. S. Filled shoeboxes can be dropped off at the church through Sunday, Nov. 22. Shetler said the boxes will travel through Kamloops to Calgary, where they’ll be checked before being shipped overseas.

The new government could also get started building other infrastructure, like the promised urgent care centres and Surrey women’s and children’s hospital. Governments and regulators are reassessing privacy safeguards, with Finland reviewing rules governing workplace communications, Hong Kong launching a support program for organisations adopting artificial intelligence, and European lawmakers debating proposed changes to data-protection law. Communities across the United States are taking different approaches to police automated license-plate reader (ALPR) networks: voters in York, Maine, and League City, Texas, rejected their use, while Cedar Rapids approved a nearly $500,000 switch from Flock Safety to Axon without increasing its network of 70 cameras. Ohio lawmakers are considering House Bill 725, which would set statewide rules for police use of plate data and make misuse a fifth-degree felony. The ACLU of Ohio argues the bill regulates data only after collection and could reduce public access to search information. Springfield’s committee plans to meet again after consulting the city’s Law Department.

items.title: [medicalxpress.com] Study links very large and small waists to higher death risk
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A study of more than 17 million South Korean adults found that both unusually large and unusually small waist measurements were associated with a higher risk of death across weight and age groups. The lowest observed risk was associated with waist circumferences of 80–94 centimeters in men and 75–89 centimeters in women. The association between waist circumference and death risk was stronger at older ages, especially among women 75 and older. Researchers analyzed routine health-check measurements from 2009–10 and tracked survival for nearly 14 years, through June 30, 2024. The study was observational and cannot show that waist size causes death. Among people with normal weight or overweight whose waist circumference was high for their body mass index (BMI), reducing waist circumference without necessarily losing weight appeared to offer a greater survival benefit than losing weight while reducing waist circumference, the authors said.

items.content_html:

The Internal Revenue Service raised federal income tax bracket thresholds for 2027, allowing taxpayers to earn more before entering a higher bracket. Tax rates remain unchanged, with the top rate still 37%. For single filers, the 22% bracket starts above $52,025 and the 37% bracket above $661,375; for married couples filing jointly, those thresholds are $104,050 and $793,650. The IRS also increased the maximum child tax credit to $2,300, including a refundable portion of up to $1,800, and raised the maximum earned income tax credit for qualifying families with at least three children to $8,496. The annual inflation adjustments are intended to keep wage increases from pushing taxpayers into higher brackets when their purchasing power has not increased.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN warns 2026 heat records signal accelerating climate extremes
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Earth’s energy imbalance has reached its highest level since monitoring began, and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says 2026 is on track to rank among the four warmest years on record. Global surface temperature averaged about 1.47°C above the preindustrial level from January through September; a developing, unusually strong El Niño could push the annual figure higher and prolong extreme heat into 2027. The agency released its report as the U.N. climate summit COP31 opened in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiations scheduled through Nov. 20. The agency says each of the past 12 years ranked among the 12 warmest on record, with 2023-2026 likely to be the four warmest years. Greenhouse gases from human activity are trapping heat; the ocean absorbs about 90% of the excess, while sea levels and ocean temperatures have reached records. The WMO warns that the accumulating heat will intensify heat waves, droughts, tropical cyclones and heavy rain. A separate U.N. Environment Programme assessment says warming will exceed 1.5°C under every plausible emissions pathway. Returning below that threshold this century would require near-zero emissions and the removal of hundreds of billions of tonnes of carbon dioxide. The WMO’s full 2026 climate report is due in March 2027.

items.title: [proplanta.de] EU convenes crisis talks as freezer hacks spread to Germany, Romania
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The European Commission convened two crisis meetings after cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems spread across Europe, with incidents reported in at least 11 countries, including Germany and Romania. The attacks remotely raised temperatures or triggered defrost cycles, forcing retailers to discard food; no group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not established whether the incidents share a perpetrator. The wave follows a similar attack on French supermarkets in October. A store in Lilienthal, Germany, said it had to discard goods worth more than €360,000, while six Romanian stores were affected. Italy’s government held talks with intelligence and cybersecurity officials and said the impact there was limited to a small number of commercial sites; it reported no health risk from thawed food. EU officials are coordinating with national authorities, who are conducting the investigations. Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc’s food supply was not currently threatened, and the Commission said the incidents showed a need for stronger cybersecurity across the EU.

items.title: [scientificamerican.com] Neanderthal DNA variant linked to smaller visual brain region, lower schizophrenia odds
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Researchers report that a Neanderthal-derived DNA variant is associated with a smaller occipital lobe and lower odds of schizophrenia in modern humans. In UK Biobank data, each copy of the variant corresponded to about 0.85 cubic centimeters less occipital-lobe volume; people with two copies had nearly 10% lower odds of schizophrenia than those with no copies. The occipital lobe processes visual information. The variant lies near DAAM1, a gene involved in brain development, but researchers have not established how it affects the brain or whether the smaller lobe explains the schizophrenia association. The variant was not associated with a meaningful difference in intelligence, and outside researchers cautioned against drawing conclusions about Neanderthal brain function from the findings in modern humans. The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Its authors say further work, including studies using brain organoids or animal models, could investigate the mechanism.
